entries.title: The Supreme Court Is Considering the Future of Climate Change Lawsuits
entries.summary: The justices hear oral arguments Monday in a major environmental case over fossil fuel company liability.
entries.content:
The Supreme Court will hear oral arguments Monday in a case that could block one of the last remaining legal paths for holding fossil fuel companies responsible for damage from climate change.

The case, Suncor Energy vs. Boulder County, centers on a procedural question of whether the companies must face lawsuits in state courts, or if federal law precludes those.

The answer could shape the future of claims from dozens of states, counties and cities seeking to use state laws to recoup billions of dollars for the costs associated with climate disasters such as fires and floods.

Other legal avenues for holding fossil fuel companies accountable have already been foreclosed, including by a 2011 Supreme Court decision that effectively left no future for similar cases in federal court.

“So if this one is closed, too, then seeking court remedies is going to be largely off the table,” said Jonathan Adler, a professor at William & Mary Law School who filed a brief in the case.

The city and county of Boulder, Colorado, filed a state lawsuit that aims to hold Suncor Energy and Exxon Mobil responsible for costs associated with climate disasters, arguing under a state law that the companies deceived the public about the danger of their products.

The Colorado Supreme Court ruled that federal law doesn’t stand in the way of the claims moving forward in state court. Similar claims have been filed across the country, including Vermont, Minnesota and Hawaii, and courts have been split on the question of whether federal law preempts the lawsuits.

Suncor Energy and Exxon Mobil told the Supreme Court in a filing in the case that the justices have a chance to address whether the climate change litigation can proceed before “the energy industry is threatened with potentially enormous judgments.”

“There are few, if any, more consequential questions pending in the lower courts concerning the relationship between state and federal law,” the companies wrote in their petition for the court to hear the case.

In an unusual move, the Supreme Court agreed to review the issue before the case has gone to trial and before a state court has made a final judgement. So the justices also will decide whether they have jurisdiction over the case at this early stage, a question that could give them a way to avoid a major decision at this time.

The Trump administration has unsuccessfully attempted to block several state law cases, suing states that are suing fossil fuel companies. Congress is also trying to weigh in: Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) introduced a bill that would expressly foreclose state claims against fossil fuel companies.

The Supreme Court has declined to look at the same question previously, last year on a lawsuit from the city and county of Honolulu, and in 2023 on the same Suncor v. Boulder case. At least four justices must agree to grant a petition.

In both of those instances, Justice Samuel Alito recused himself early in the process, leaving the other eight justices to decide whether the court should take up the case. Alito owns stock ConocoPhillips and Phillips 66, companies implicated in related cases.

This time around, Alito did not recuse himself early on, and the court decided to take up the case. But this week, the conservative justice reversed course, recusing himself with a one-sentence announcement from the Supreme Court clerk.

Across the country, climate-related cases against fossil fuel companies vary in terms of their legal claims and the remedies they’re asking the court to provide. But the basic facts are the same, said Corey Riday-White, the legal director of the Center for Climate Integrity.

“They knew, they lied, they should be held accountable,” he said.

Riday-White likened Boulder’s case to those involving tobacco companies, opioid manufacturers and Meta. “You have companies that promote and sell a harmful product without warning the public about those harms, and the courts are the proper venue to go to to get compensated for those harms,” he said.

Suncor Energy and Exxon Mobil argue Boulder’s lawsuit amounts to an attempt to regulate its emissions across the country and the globe — a role only federal law can take.

The companies, in their brief, called the variety of claims against fossil fuel firms “complete chaos,” and said using state law to address climate change “represents a serious threat to one of our Nation’s most critical sectors.”

Saikrishna Prakash, a professor at the University of Virginia School of Law, argues in a brief filed in the case that Boulder is attempting to regulate fossil fuel production across the United States. Prakash contends that allowing the lawsuit to move forward would create a slippery slope to local governments being allowed to regulate consumers of fossil fuels, such as regular Americans who use gas stoves.

“[Boulder’s] lawsuit reflects a desire to change the world and rests on a long-arm theory of regulatory power, where Colorado may regulate worldwide to stem the effects of greenhouse gas emissions,” Prakash wrote.

Boulder argues in court filings that the federal government is not charged with regulating the “deceptive marketing” of fossil fuels. And it asserts that if the Supreme Court ruled that the Clean Air Act preempted any state laws that indirectly affect emissions, that would negatively affect everything from state gasoline taxes to local energy-efficiency regulations.

Historically, greenhouse gas emissions have been regulated under the Clean Air Act. But this year, the Environmental Protection Agency rescinded the endangerment finding, which provided the basis for the federal government’s ability to regulate emissions under that law.

EPA officials from Republican and Democratic administrations filed a brief arguing that consumer protection and deceptive advertising lawsuits like Boulder’s are not preempted by the Clean Air Act.

Dozens of other amici briefs have been filed, including from members of Congress, climate economists, city and county governments, manufacturing and transportation trade groups and the Justice Department.

In one, a group of Colorado ranchers explains how climate change has affected their livelihoods. One rancher said she had to sell all the cattle on her third-generation ranch after a wildfire ripped through in 2025. Another said his cattle didn’t have enough drinking water and were unable to graze their usual pastures.

“They fear that if municipal government keeps absorbing the increasing costs imposed by heat, drought, fires, and flooding, it will not be able to provide the services on which they depend to continue ranching,” their brief said.

Deirdre Macnab, a cattle rancher who learned about the case from her local newspaper, said she’s watched climate change take a toll on her neighbors and her own ranch, recalling fires that killed 60 of her neighbor’s cattle and took out miles of fences and transmission lines.

“Changing climate is happening, really, before our eyes,” she said. “A very significant part of climate change is tied to the fossil fuel companies, and I believe it’s critically important, and government’s role, to hold them accountable if they’re not holding themselves accountable.”
entries.author: Mara Hoplamazian

entries.title: Capitals Fall to Lightning, 3-1, in Second Game of Season
entries.summary: Washington played the third period without defenseman Matt Roy, who suffered a lower-body injury and did not return.
entries.content:
TAMPA, Fla. — Andrei Vasilevskiy made 19 saves, Charle-Edouard D’Astous and Conor Geekie scored in the first period and the Tampa Bay Lightning won their home opener with a 3-1 victory over the Washington Capitals on Saturday night.

Brandon Hagel had two assists for the Lightning, and Jake Guentzel scored into an empty net and had an assist. Tampa Bay opened play Thursday night in New York with a 5-1 loss to the Rangers.

Charlie Lindgren finished with 27 saves for Washington. Justin Sourdif scored for the Capitals.

D’Astous put Tampa Bay up 1-0 at 2:26 of the opening period as he cut down from the point into the middle slot to take a pass from Brandon Hagel and zipped a wrist shot past Lindgren.

The Lightning finished off the period with a goal from Geekie, who was off the right wing side to take a pass from Hagel for a quick shot to the inside of the post with 3:30 top go for a 2-0 lead.

The Capitals, who opened Friday with a win in Carolina, cut the deficit in half in the second period on a redirect from Sourdif off a point shot from Jacob Chychurn.

Guentzel scored with 2:05 left in the third.

Washington played the third period without defenseman Matt Roy, who suffered a lower-body injury and did not return.

Tampa Bay defenseman John Carlson, who spent 17 seasons with the Capitals, played his first career game against Washington, picking up an assist on the empty-net goal.
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: Maryland Loses Big to Nebraska, 48-23
entries.summary: The Terps led early, but a pick-six sparked a Cornhuskers run in the defeat, which only further ratchets up the pressure on coach Mike Locksley.
entries.content:
LINCOLN, Neb. — Dwayne McDougle III’s 81-yard interception return for a touchdown sparked Nebraska in the first half, and the Cornhuskers all but shut down Maryland after that in a penalty-filled 48-23 victory Saturday.

The Cornhuskers (5-0, 2-0 Big Ten) are out to their best start since 2016 with defending national champion and sixth-ranked Indiana coming to Memorial Stadium next week.

The Terrapins (2-3, 0-2), a week removed from a 54-3 home loss to UCLA, led most of the first half before seeing the game turn on the third pick-6 thrown by Malik Washington over four quarters. Their 18th loss in 20 Big Ten games only increased the pressure on eighth-year coach Mike Locksley.

Without injured running back Jamal Rule, quarterback Anthony Colandrea had the first 100-yard rushing game of his career, going for 108 on 10 carries. He was 26-of-39 passing for 238 yards and three touchdowns. Kwazi Gilmer had career highs of 11 catches for 147 yards and two TDs.

“The way we play, it’s maybe not all the time the coolest thing, the visual, but we’re going to try to be physical,” Nebraska coach Matt Rhule said. “Sometimes we might go three and out, but if we continue to be physical, we give ourselves a chance in the fourth quarter.”

Washington was 23 of 44 for 254 yards and a touchdown, and his two interceptions increased his season total to six, all in the last two games. Chris Durr Jr. caught seven passes for 149 yards and a TD.

The Huskers were down 23-14 midway through the second quarter when McDougle stepped in front of Washington’s pass intended for Kaleb Webb and ran it back all the way for Nebraska’s longest pick-6 since 2007.

“I was playing off the quarterback, and as soon as he pulled the trigger, I knew I was taking it the other way,” McDougle said.

Washington’s three pick-6s over four quarters are the most over such a short span since Kyle McCord threw three in the first two quarters against Pittsburgh on Oct. 24, 2024, according to Sportradar.

Colandrea passed one yard to Luke Lindenmeyer to finish a quick eight-play, 80-yard drive that put the Huskers in front 28-23 at half, and Gilmer’s TD catches of 5 and 30 yards pushed the lead to 25 points.

Maryland totaled 300 yards of offense in the first half and just 62 the rest of the way.

“I can’t complain about the effort and the energy we started the game with,” Locksley said. “Make no make no mistake about that. I thought they came and approached this team with the right mentality, but had way too many self-inflicted wounds. And when you play good teams like Nebraska, they don’t need help.”
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: Trump Launches ‘Super Intelligence Force’ to Lead AI Coordination
entries.summary: The head of national intelligence, the chair of the FTC and officials from the Pentagon and personnel management will lead the force.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump announced the creation of a “Super Intelligence Force” to lead the federal government’s response to AI innovation.

“The Super Intelligence Force is tasked with coordinating the effort of the Federal Government to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence, which many say is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the Internet, and will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans,” Trump wrote Sunday on Truth Social.

Trump tapped Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton to lead the task force alongside Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson, under secretary of defense for research and engineering Emil Michael, and the director of the Office of Personnel Management, Scott Kupor.

In a Time interview released last week, Trump said the Super Intelligence Force would be made up of “very smart people that understand it, who will be advising me.”

The leaders of the group will continue serving in their current posts while taking on their roles on the new task force.

David Sacks was the Trump administration’s crypto and AI czar before leaving in March after reaching the 130-day limit for special government employees.

Clayton, who took over as head of the U.S. intelligence community in August, is stepping into the position as Washington has been roiled by debate over how much oversight the AI industry needs. He has argued that the government already has tools to address AI-related harms.

“We have consumer protection laws. We have product liability laws,” Clayton said Wednesday on CNBC. He also pointed to the Justice Department as part of the government’s existing framework for dealing with AI.

In recent weeks, leaders at Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceXAI have urged AI companies to slow the development of their most powerful models to allow more time for safeguards, warning they could be misused for cyberattacks and eventually outpace human control.

Trump met Tuesday at the White House with leaders of major tech companies. Six companies — Google, Anthropic, Meta, OpenAI, SpaceXAI and Nvidia — signed a voluntary safety accord. Trump said they would “self-police” and take responsibility for developing their technology safely. He called the agreement “morally binding,” though it imposes no legal requirements on the companies.

But lawmakers from both parties are pushing for more accountability, including a bipartisan bill from Sens. Josh Hawley (R-Missouri) and Chris Murphy (D-Connecticut) that would hold AI developers and operators liable for hacking incidents involving AI agents.

Trump signed an executive order on Sept. 22 officially rebranding “AI” as “Super Intelligence,” or “SI,” across the executive branch.
entries.author: Hamed Ahmadi, Jenna Monnin

entries.title: Alito Defends Justices Against a ‘Concerted Effort to Intimidate the Court’
entries.summary: President Donald Trump said last week that he regretted nominating several conservative justices after they “voted against me too often.”
entries.content:
Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito defended the high court from a “concerted effort to intimidate” the institution after he was asked about President Donald Trump and other groups calling out his fellow justices by name over some of their decisions and talk of reforming the court.

When asked specifically about Trump’s Truth Social post condemning several conservative justices for rejecting his push to restrict mail-in voting ahead of the midterms, Alito expressed his concerns about the “escalating” discourse from those in "important positions.”

“I put all of that out of my mind. I trust that my colleagues put all of that out of their minds, but I am concerned about the escalation in public rhetoric in general, and about the things that people in important positions say about the Supreme Court as a whole and about individual justices,” Alito said in a rare sit-down interview with Fox News. “I'm concerned about the long-term effect of that on the standing of the court.”

Although he didn’t mention them by name, Trump lambasted Justices Neil Gorsuch, Amy Coney Barrett and Brett Kavanaugh for their decision to side with the majority of the court and block Trump’s new regulations for mail-in ballots. When asked specifically if he regretted nominating those three justices in a recent interview with Time Magazine, Trump said he did because they “voted against me too often.”

“These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court, they are merely a shell of their original selves,” Trump wrote in a Sept. 15 Truth Social post.

Trump directly praised Alito and Justice Clarence Thomas for dissenting in the case, calling them “legends.”

Alito spoke about a broader effort to “intimidate” the court when asked about the push for adding term- or age-limits to the Supreme Court reforms, but said he does not discuss the potential reforms with his colleagues when they come up publicly.

“There has been a concerted effort to intimidate the court and justices on the court try to influence us to decide cases differently from the way in which we have been deciding them, and I am concerned about the future of the court,” Alito said.

Alito sat down with Fox News host Shannon Bream ahead of the release of his new book "So Ordered: An Originalist's View of the Constitution, the Court, and Our Country.” The pair discussed how Alito’s views as an originalist — which means he believes any issue before the court should be interpreted based on how it was understood at the time it was adopted — can reconcile with issues the Founding Fathers never imagined when writing the constitution, such as artificial intelligence or surveillance.

“Those are the most difficult cases,” Alito said. “But when you're dealing with something like new technology, history cannot provide that kind of an answer, and so in those instances, the best we can do is to try to understand as clearly as we can the legal principle that is embodied in the Constitution, and then we have to apply that to this new technology and try to apply it in the way that makes the most sense.”

The justice has faced some pressure from Republicans to retire, as the party would be able to more easily push through a Supreme Court nomination while it has control of the Senate.

“I've been amused by the retirement speculation,” Alito said. “It's not too pleasant to look up and see the vultures circling around your head. But the speculation is to be expected. It's what goes with life tenure.”

Alito told CBS News in an interview this week that he thought about retiring at the end of the last term and will reconsider retirement each year.

The justice wrote the 2022 majority opinion overturning Roe v. Wade, and he has become one of the court’s staunchest conservatives after being nominated by President George W. Bush in 2005.

When asked about whether or not his Catholic faith opens him up for criticism on abortion-access decisions and other cultural issues, Alito responded by saying he is “not biased” and all decisions must be rooted in the law.

“I think we all, all judges, and certainly all justices, must decide cases that have implications for their personal beliefs.” Alito said. “They could be philosophical beliefs, political beliefs, economic beliefs, or religious beliefs, but we must make a very concerted effort not to base our decisions on our personal beliefs.”
entries.author: Jenna Monnin

entries.title: Commanders Lose to Colts in London, 30-13, After Another QB Injury
entries.summary: Rookie Athan Kaliakmanis replaced Marcus Mariota, who was starting in place of Jayden Daniels, after he left with a knee injury in the first half.
entries.content:
LONDON — It was already going to be a tall task for the Commanders to escape London with a victory over the Colts without starting quarterback Jayden Daniels and top receiver Terry McLaurin.

But losing several additional players throughout the game, including quarterback Marcus Mariota, proved to be too much in a 30-13 loss for Washington that dropped them to 1-3 on the season.

The Commanders, coming off a spirited upset of the defending champion Seahawks last week, lost Mariota on the second drive of the game to a knee injury. They then lost defensive end Charles Omenihu at the end of the first quarter, and returner Jaylin Lane and safety Jeremy Reaves within two minutes of each other at the start of the second half.

It looked like the team could weather the previous injuries early on. The defense allowed one total yard through the first three Colts possessions, including a strip-sack and fumble recovery by edge rusher Odafe Oweh. With just under two minutes left in the second quarter, Colts quarterback Daniel Jones was pressured into throwing an interception to cornerback Rasul Douglas.

But even with Mariota in the game, the offense struggled. They were gifted the ball at Indianapolis’ 21-yard line after the Oweh fumble recovery but moved the ball just 8 yards and settled for a Drew Stevens field goal. On their next possession they marched 70 yards down the field but the drive stalled when Mariota was sacked on third down on the play in which he was injured, leading to another Stevens field goal.

A turnover on downs midway through the second quarter led to a Jonathan Taylor touchdown. And Athan Kaliakmanis, filling in for Mariota, threw an interception 51 seconds into the start of the second half.

The rookie did have some impressive moments, however, including a beautifully thrown 47-yard touchdown bomb to Treylon Burks in the third quarter that kept Washington in the game. The seventh-round pick out of Rutgers finished the game with 186 yards, one touchdown and one interception on 15-of-33 passing.

But by the end of the third quarter the team was worn down. The defense — which had performed well most of the game — allowed a nine-play, 52-yard drive at the top of the fourth quarter that put the game out of reach.

This story will update.
entries.author: Martenzie Johnson

entries.title: Jayden Daniels’ Return Just Went From a Luxury to a Necessity
entries.summary: The Commanders’ season is hanging by a thread following Sunday’s 30-13 loss to the Colts, making their star QB’s return next week even more essential.
entries.content:
When the Washington Commanders decided late last week to keep starting quarterback Jayden Daniels sidelined for another week out of caution for the left elbow he dislocated two weeks ago in Dallas, it was a choice made from a position of relative luxury: in veteran Marcus Mariota, the Commanders had one of the best backup quarterbacks in the NFL, one who had just led them to a season-saving upset win over the defending Super Bowl champions the week before.

It is a luxury that now appears to have vanished — along with whatever momentum and good vibes carried over from last week — during Sunday’s dispiriting 30-13 loss to the Indianapolis Colts at London’s Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.

With Mariota now lost for an undetermined amount of time thanks to a knee injury suffered on a sack late in Sunday’s first quarter (coach Dan Quinn said postgame that the team will know after tests Monday how long he’ll be out), the complex calculus governing Daniels’s return to action now carries an urgency and immediacy that didn’t exist before that fateful play.

The Commanders (1-3) no longer merely prefer that Daniels is able to return next week at home against the NFC East rival New York Giants. If there still any hope of salvaging this season, they absolutely, positively, 100 percent need him to.

You typically don’t want decisions involving injured players to be influenced by positional need, particularly when it comes to your franchise quarterback, but in a brutal sport where legacies and jobs are riding on every game, the temptation is always to be aggressive. That’s not to suggest the Commanders would push Daniels to play before he’s ready, but in the absence of Mariota as a palatable Plan B against the Giants, it would only be natural for the team’s sheer plight at the position to influence that calculus.

“That's the hope for us for sure, Jay coming back [next week],” Quinn said. “He'll have a full week of practice Wednesday, Thursday, Friday. That's the goal that he could get into that space.”

It’s not as if third-stringer Athan Kaliakmanis, a rookie and seventh-round draft pick out of Rutgers, was a disaster when pressed into duty Sunday. He showed flashes of the big arm and the poise that attracted them to him in the first place, mixing in a handful of well-thrown deep balls among his 15-of-33, 186-yard, one-touchdown, one-interception performance against the Colts. He also had an apparent 87-yard touchdown to fellow rookie Antonio Williams called back for an illegal motion penalty.

“He showed a lot of confidence, some fearlessness,” Quinn said of Kaliakmanis. “I don’t think we did enough around him.”

But there is a reason seventh-rounders rarely turn into serviceable NFL quarterbacks, with the most prominent exceptions being Brock Purdy and Ryan Fitzpatrick. And if it turns out the Commanders harbor any doubts about Daniels’s readiness for Week 5, they would be smart to look into signing a stopgap veteran until he’s ready rather than rely on Kaliakmanis against the Giants.

Things got this bad for the Commanders on Sunday, who weren’t carrying a third quarterback on their active roster: for more than three quarters — with Daniels in a street clothes on the sideline, Mariota in the care of the team’s medical staff and Kaliakmanis absorbing some big hits in the pocket — they were one awkward fall away from seeing Colson Yankoff, a fourth-string tight end and special teams ace who had been a highly regarded quarterback prospect in high school, pressed into duty as their emergency signal-caller.

(Speaking of tight ends, that position was supposed to have been a strength for the Commanders this season following the signing of veteran Chig Okonkwo, who has three 50-catch seasons on his resume. But on Sunday, the entire tight end room was outgained in receiving yards by left tackle Brandon Coleman, who rumbled for 13 yards and a first down after hauling in a batted pass during the game’s waning moments.)

It certainly didn’t help either Mariota nor Kaliakmanis on Sunday that the Commanders’ offense was also without top wideout Terry McLaurin (hamstring), third-down back Rachaad White (shoulder) as well as their two top linemen, Laremy Tunsil (torn triceps, likely out for the season) and Sam Cosmi (concussion). A clean, clutch performance from the offense still might have made it a game down the stretch, but the Commanders torpedoed their own hopes with 10 penalties for 84 yards – a mix of inexcusable mistakes and questionable officiating – and a 3-for-19 showing on third- and fourth-down tries.

Daniels, meantime, prowled the sidelines Sunday, a sight that has become all too familiar these past two seasons, during which he has missed a total of 12 games. He wore a headset under his hood to listen in on the Commanders’ play-calls and a bulky elbow brace under his left sleeve, presumably to help him get used to wearing it on the field once he returns. He frequently sauntered over to Kaliakmanis between offensive series, offering support and encouragement.

“I think Jayden Daniels is the ultimate leader, coaching me throughout the entire game. That’s what a true pro looks like in my eyes,” Kaliakmanis told reporters. “... He’s coaching me, giving me hints and stuff like that about the game, what the defense might be doing, play-call recommendations. I couldn’t be more thankful for a guy like that.”

The Commanders’ first-half schedule, meantime, is unrelenting. After the resurgent Giants on Sunday, they travel to San Francisco for a Monday night game against the 49ers in Week 6 before reaching their bye week. Finding a way to at least split those two games would seem to be the bare minimum requirement for keeping their season hopes alive – because coming out of the bye, they have the Philadelphia Eagles and Los Angeles Rams, both playoff teams last season.

“I really believe in these guys,” Quinn said. “... I think a good fire’s been lit and it will stay lit. I have high expectations of what we can be, despite the start [to the season] we’ve had. It has not dampened my belief in them in any way. It is difficult to overcome some of the injuries. But I’m certain these are the right guys to battle for it.”

At 1-3, the Commanders’ season is on the edge of the same abyss it collapsed into in 2025, and for many of the same reasons. This time, thanks in large part to a defense that has been dependable for most of the past four weeks, there is still a defined pathway for them to put themselves in playoff contention by the time the schedule eases in the second half.

But it is a narrow and perilous pathway:

Get McLaurin and Cosmi back from injuries.

Clean up the penalties and the other mistakes.

And most importantly, pray that Daniels is healthy enough to get back on the field — without regard to how desperately the Commanders need him — and that once he’s back, he stays there.
entries.author: Dave Sheinin

entries.title: Sen. Kennedy Teases Potential 2028 Presidential Run
entries.summary: The Lousiana Republican said he’d consider jumping in the race “if a bunch of goobers run.”
entries.content:
Sen. John Kennedy said he would consider jumping in the 2028 presidential race if he does not like his party’s options for the Republican nominee.

“On my side of the aisle, if a bunch of goobers run, and I think they’re goobers, and one of the goobers might win, and I think I could do a better job, I would consider running,” Kennedy said Sunday on NBC’s “Meet the Press.”

The Louisiana Republican said his focus is squarely on his Senate race in 2028, but he would consider a bid for president if he doesn’t think he “can be effective in the Senate anymore.”

Kennedy, who is not up for reelection this year, has made several out-of-state appearances on the campaign trail this cycle to stump for his fellow Republicans — traveling to Iowa, Kansas and Nebraska in September and New Hampshire in June.

The senator told reporters earlier this month that he never expected to spend time in the trio of states he visited in September to drum up support for the Republican Senate candidates.

“If you told me six months ago I was going to be having to spend my time in those three states, I wouldn’t have believed you. Those ought to be fat guy layups for us,” Kennedy said, according to The Washington Post.

Kennedy, known for his frequent folksy and viral one-liners, has broken with President Donald Trump on several key issues. The Louisiana Republican publicly disagreed with Trump’s assertion that Ukraine started the war with Russia and also pushed back on the Trump administration’s deportation of Kilmar Abrego Garcia, labeling it a “screw up.”

Most recently, Kennedy criticized Trump for giving out Sen. Tom Cotton’s (R-Arkansas) cellphone number Saturday on Truth Social over the senator’s opposition to a bill that would make Daylight Saving Time permanent.

“He can be tempestuous. He can go from zero to a-hole in about three seconds,” Kennedy told NBC News about Trump. “I don’t think he should have given out Tom’s cell phone number. I don’t think that’s going to help convince Tom.”

Kennedy is in the middle of his second term in the Senate, and has never run for president.

Recent polling from YouGov puts Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis among the top names Republicans would consider voting for in 2028.
entries.author: Jenna Monnin

entries.title: U.S. Monitoring Reports of Russian Lab Worker’s Suspected Plague Death
entries.summary: The State Department called on Russian authorities to release “accurate information quickly and openly” about the developing situation.
entries.content:
The U.S. government is actively monitoring a suspected outbreak of the plague in Russia following the death of a 28-year-old lab worker who was reportedly infected after coming into contact with a broken test tube containing the pathogen.

“We are aware of reports of a fatal case of suspected pneumonic plague in Irkutsk Oblast, Russia,” a State Department spokesperson told The Washington Sun in a statement Sunday. “We are monitoring the situation closely with the CDC and our other interagency partners.”

The State Department spokesperson also called on “Russian authorities to share accurate information quickly and openly,” and said that cases of the plague are “treatable with common antibiotics, especially when treatment starts early.”

Russia is already designated by the State Department as a Level 4 “do not travel” country, but the spokesperson encouraged U.S. citizens traveling abroad to enroll in its Smart Traveler Enrollment Program to receive updates.

A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services confirmed that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is working with the State Department to address the developing situation and added that “the safety and security of U.S. citizens is our highest priority.”

The White House is also monitoring the situation and the quarantines in Russia, Axios reported Sunday. The White House and CDC did not immediately respond to The Sun’s request for comment.

Rospotrebnadzor, Russia’s national public health and consumer protection agency, wrote in a statement Sunday to Interfax — a privately owned news agency in Russia — that the lab technician was diagnosed with "pneumonia of unknown etiology" and described the situation in the Irkutsk Region, an area located in southeastern Siberia, as “stable.”

Independent Siberian news outlet Lyudi Baikala identified the patient as 28-year-old Darya Shipilova, who worked as a lab technician at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute. The outlet also reported that Shipilova allegedly broke a tube containing the pneumonic plague pathogen on Sept. 25 — an account Rospotrebnadzor has not yet publicly corroborated.

Subsequent tests run “due to the patient's professional activities,” did not identify the plague pathogen, and tests on quarantined individuals who had been in contact with the patient only found “two cases of Covid-19 and two cases of rhinovirus infection,” according to Rospotrebnadzor.

Izvestia, a Russian state-aligned media outlet, reported that at least 197 people who may have had contact with Shipilova have been placed under medical isolation.

This story has been updated to include a comment from HHS.
entries.author: Jenna Monnin

entries.title: U.S. Redeploys Bombers From British Base Targeted by Suspected Terrorists
entries.summary: The B-1 bombers will return to their home bases in the United States, the Pentagon said.
entries.content:
By Konstantin Toropin

The U.S. Air Force has brought home its bombers stationed at a U.S.-run military air base in England used to strike Iran following an investigation into a planned terror attack at the RAF Fairford base.

The bombers were redeployed back to their home bases in the United States, according to a Pentagon official who was not authorized to discuss sensitive military movements and spoke Sunday on condition of anonymity.

Aviation watchers such as the Military Air Tracking Alliance have observed dozens of B-52 and B-1 bombers operating out of RAF Fairford since the opening days of the Iran war. Observers noticed a host of B-1 bombers fly out of the base on Sunday.

A dual British-Iranian national was arrested in central London last week on suspicion of plotting a terror attack, following a security incident at RAF Fairford in late September. In total, six people have been taken into custody and then released on bail during the investigation.

British authorities have linked the incident to Tehran. Iran has denied involvement.

RAF Fairford, located 100 miles (160 kilometers) west of London, has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East.

The U.S. military still maintains a sizable presence in the Middle East. On Thursday, a U.S. official said the recently deployed USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier, as well as the USS Malkin Island amphibious readiness group — a group of ships that together carry over 7,000 sailors and 2,000 Marines — are heading for the region. The official said the move could result in three carriers in the region as early as the end of October.
